headline: Hold at high 30s PE; new foldable iPhone exciting under hardware-focused CEO but priced forward, and Google more attractive on comparative valuation
reasoning: Mark Moreland has held Apple for ~20 years as a 10X investment compounding at over 26% annually, but flags the stock is expensive at a high-30s PE versus peers. He is cautious on the foldable iPhone given the $3,000+ AUD price point and consumer breakage risk. He is intrigued by the new CEO John Turnus who comes from a hardware background rather than the 'farming/milking' approach of recent years, but says he has to prove himself. Apple's AI strategy via a Gemini deal also remains a challenge. On a comparative basis, he prefers Google, which trades around 17x PE with cloud revenue growing 38-84% and higher earnings growth; he would put fresh money into Google over Apple but is not selling Apple.
quote: I think the the iPhone, the folding iPhones taking a long time... for me, Apple as a whole, I think the John Tienis new CEO who's come from a hardware background versus the basically the farming mode they've been in for years, just milking it, I think is potentially very exciting. But he's got to prove that what he's going to do. And there's a major software challenges they have as well, which is how they deal with AI and they've done a deal with Gemini. I think the market's been very positive to them on their pricing, but it is a little bit forward from my point of view. Whereas if you look at Google particularly, I think it's on AP of 17 or something at the moment. And they've got they're growing like the cloud business has been growing at 38 percent, 84% last year. And their their earnings growth is way higher than Apple. So if you look at it comparatively, if I was going to put money into one right now, I would go Google. I'm not selling Apple. So I'd call it a hold.

headline: Mark Moreland sees Netflix as cheap on historical valuation multiples and would look to buy after earnings, though flags content quality and gaming diversification as risks.
reasoning: Moreland notes Netflix trades at around 23x earnings versus a historical average of roughly 40x, which he views as a meaningful discount making it potentially attractive. He acknowledges user engagement is declining and that original content quality has softened, which are the key investor concerns. He is skeptical about the gaming pivot, questioning whether it suits Netflix's platform DNA. On the positive side he points to growing advertising revenue as a tailwind, and says if one were to buy, now is not a bad time — though he would wait until after the earnings release.
quote: You know, it's one of the biggest, largest streaming platforms. There are 300 million users on there. But again, as Mark alluded to, it's more about user engagement at the moment, because I think a lot of the investors are worried that the original content that was on Netflix before, that's really what blew it up... in terms of gaming, I don't know if it's the right thing to do because it just to me, that doesn't seem the right route. Like, how does how do people engage with Netflix on a gaming platform? It's not the domain they're usually in. Um, so it's a tangent, but I don't know how well that will play off. It's a risk as well. Um, one positive is that the advertising revenue is going up... valuations really cheap. So compared to historical at about 40 or so it's at 23. So it is you know, it is discounted at the moment. And you know, if you were going to buy it, it's actually not a bad time to buy it. I would wait till after earnings release.

headline: Micron described as interesting but second preference to SK Hynix as a memory cycle play
